name: Exterior Sprinkler Systems
tagline: Keep your roof, walls and the 1.5 m around your home wet when embers arrive.
intro: Exterior sprinkler kits mount on gutters, roof peaks or tripods and wet down the structure and immediate zone ahead of a fire front. Consumer kits run off a garden hose or a gas-powered pump drawing from a pool, pond or tank. They are the single most effective product-based defense a homeowner can add — but only if you have a water source that keeps working when municipal pressure drops.
buyingNotes: Water source matters more than the sprinkler. Municipal pressure often collapses during a wildfire; a pump plus a pool, cistern or IBC tote is the resilient setup.
Look for brass or metal sprinkler heads and UV-rated hose — plastic heads fail in radiant heat.
Gutter-mounted kits (WASP-style) are the fastest DIY install; roof-peak kits cover more surface but need a ladder and hardware.
Coverage is rated in metres/feet of radius per head. Measure your roofline and buy 20% more heads than the math says.
Turn on early — 30 to 60 minutes before the front arrives — and keep an eye on your water budget.

name: Fire Retardant Gel & Spray
tagline: Coat siding, decks and fences with a protective barrier before you evacuate.
intro: Fire-blocking gels and long-term retardant sprays create a heat-absorbing barrier on wood, vinyl and composite surfaces. Gels (Barricade, Thermo-Gel, FireIce) are applied with a hose-end sprayer minutes before evacuation and last several hours. Long-term retardants (Phos-Chek Home Defense) are applied days or weeks ahead and stay effective until washed off by rain.
buyingNotes: Gels are a last-minute product: apply when evacuation is ordered, not the week before. They dry out in 6–24 hours depending on heat and wind.
Long-term retardants are seasonal: apply to fences, decks and mulch beds in early fire season and refresh after heavy rain.
A 5-gallon (19 L) gel concentrate typically covers a 2,000 sq ft (185 m²) home exterior. Buy two if you have outbuildings.
Check the applicator: hose-end sprayers need ~40 psi. If your pressure drops in an emergency, a backpack sprayer is more reliable.
Gel is not a substitute for sprinklers — it protects surfaces from radiant heat and embers, but it does not stop a crown fire.

name: Ember-Resistant Vents
tagline: Most homes are lost to embers that get inside — not to flames.
intro: Wind-driven embers can travel over a kilometre ahead of the fire front and enter through attic, soffit, gable, foundation and dryer vents. Ember-resistant vents use fine metal mesh (1/8 in / 3 mm or smaller), baffles, or intumescent coatings that expand and seal at high temperatures. Replacing vents is one of the highest-return hardening jobs you can do for a few hundred dollars.
buyingNotes: Look for WUI-listed (California Wildland-Urban Interface, ASTM E2886) products. That listing is the benchmark everywhere, including Canada.
Mesh size is critical: 1/8 in (3 mm) blocks embers while still allowing airflow. 1/16 in (1.6 mm) clogs with debris and is discouraged.
Measure every existing vent opening before ordering — sizes vary by builder and era.
Don't forget the dryer vent, the range hood exhaust and any gable-end louvres.
If replacement isn't possible, stainless 1/8 in mesh screening retrofitted over existing vents is the budget alternative.

name: Gutter Guards & Roof Protection
tagline: A gutter full of dry needles is a fuse leading straight into your attic.
intro: Gutters collect exactly the fuel embers love: dry leaves, pine needles and twigs. Metal gutter guards keep them clean, and non-combustible gutter and downspout materials keep a small ignition from spreading to the eave. Pair this category with ember-resistant vents to close off the roofline.
buyingNotes: Choose metal (steel or aluminum) guards. Plastic and foam inserts melt and can ignite.
Micro-mesh guards block needles; larger perforated guards let pine needles through. Match to your trees.
If you have vinyl gutters, plan to replace with aluminum — vinyl drops burning material onto siding.
Roof sprinklers and gutter guards conflict on some profiles; check compatibility if you're buying both.
Clean gutters at the start of fire season regardless of guards.

name: Fire Blankets & Structure Wraps
tagline: Aluminized wraps reflect radiant heat — used by the US Forest Service on historic cabins.
intro: Structure wrap is a fibreglass or silica fabric with an aluminized face, stapled over an entire building to reflect radiant heat and block embers. It's labour-intensive and best suited to small buildings, sheds, and propane tanks. Personal fire blankets and fire-escape blankets belong in every kitchen and go-bag regardless.
buyingNotes: Structure wrap needs 2–4 people and several hours to install; buy it well before fire season and rehearse the install.
Wrap must overlap and be sealed at every seam and edge — embers find gaps.
Small propane tank covers are cheap and worthwhile; propane tanks venting near a home are a major ignition source.
Kitchen fire blankets (1 m × 1 m fibreglass) are not wildfire products but should be in every home.
Personal fire shelters (as used by wildland crews) are a last resort and require training — they are not a substitute for evacuating early.

name: Pumps, Hoses & Water Storage
tagline: When the hydrants go dry, your pump is the only pressure you have.
intro: A portable gas or battery fire pump drawing from a pool, pond, cistern or tank is the backbone of a serious home defense setup. Combined with fire hose, a nozzle and an exterior sprinkler kit, it gives you 30–90 minutes of protection regardless of what the municipal system is doing.
buyingNotes: Match pump output (GPM / LPM) to your sprinkler kit's total demand plus one hose line.
Gas pumps are the standard; keep fuel stabilized and test-run monthly in fire season.
A 1,000–2,500 gallon (4,000–10,000 L) poly tank is the practical minimum for a sprinkler-defended home without a pool.
Use 1.5 in fire hose with camlock or NH-threaded fittings — garden hose kinks and melts.
Store the pump, hose and fittings in one pre-connected kit. In an evacuation you will not have time to hunt for adapters.

name: Defensible Space & Yard Tools
tagline: The first 10 metres decide whether your house survives.
intro: FireSmart Canada and NFPA Firewise both emphasise the same thing: what's within 1.5 m of the house should be non-combustible, and 1.5–10 m should be thinned, limbed and cleared of ladder fuels. The tools here are ordinary — rakes, pole saws, chippers — but buying them with wildfire in mind changes what you prioritize.
buyingNotes: Priority one is Zone 0 (0–1.5 m): replace bark mulch with rock, move firewood and propane away, clear under decks.
A pole saw for limbing conifers to 2 m from the ground is the highest-leverage tool you can buy.
Battery tools are fine for maintenance; a small gas chipper pays for itself if you're thinning a treed lot.
Buy a steel leaf rake and a McLeod (fire rake) — dry needle accumulation is the fuel you'll be fighting all season.
Non-combustible mulch (crushed rock, pea gravel) is a product too — plan delivery early in the season.
A 19 L (5 gallon) backpack pump is the wildland-crew tool for spot fires in mulch, decks and grass, and it is the one piece of firefighting kit worth having for the yard.

name: Home Extinguishers
tagline: The right extinguisher in the right room, and an honest look at the gadgets sold beside it.
intro: A portable extinguisher is for a fire small enough to fight in its first minute, with a clear way out behind you. For a home that means a listed ABC unit of real size (not a 1 kg toy) in the kitchen, the garage and on each floor, plus knowing when to leave instead. Beside them on the shelf sit aerosol cans, throwable fire balls and other gadgets; we review those too, and most of them do not replace a listed extinguisher.
buyingNotes: Buy listed extinguishers: UL-listed in the US, ULC-listed in Canada. The rating on the label (for example 2-A:10-B:C) tells you what it is tested to put out.
A 2.5 kg (5 lb) ABC unit is the practical minimum for a kitchen; a 4.5 kg (10 lb) unit belongs in the garage and workshop.
Mount it near an exit, not beside the stove, so you can fight the fire with your escape route behind you.
Check the gauge monthly and replace disposable units after any use or once they reach the end of the life printed on them.
Aerosol cans and fire balls are not listed as fire extinguishers. Treat them as extras, never as the extinguisher for a room.

name: Smoke & Carbon Monoxide Alarms
tagline: The cheapest thing in your house that has ever saved a life.
intro: A working smoke alarm roughly halves the death rate per house fire, and the single most common reason one fails is that somebody took the battery out. That one fact should shape everything you buy here: pick the design that removes the human step. Hardwired and interconnected is best, a sealed ten-year lithium unit is the best retrofit, and a nine-volt you have to remember to change is the worst of the three. Alarms are also the one category with real law attached, and the law differs by province and state.
buyingNotes: Replace the whole alarm ten years from its date of manufacture, not just the battery. Check the date printed on the back — most people have at least one unit that is older than they think.

Carbon monoxide sensors wear out faster than smoke sensors, typically around seven years. That mismatch is the real drawback of a combination unit: its useful life is governed by whichever sensor expires first.

Ionisation responds faster to flaming fires, photoelectric to smouldering ones. The current advice from USFA is to have both technologies or a dual-sensor alarm, but the better filter now is whether the unit meets the current UL 217 standard, which tests both fire types and cooking nuisance.

Placement is code, not preference: one on every storey including the basement, one inside each bedroom, and one in the hallway serving them. Keep photoelectric units at least 6 ft from the stove and ionisation units at least 20 ft, or you will be taking the battery out by March.
Smoke alarms belong on the ceiling; CO alarms are usually wall-mounted and 5 to 15 ft from fuel-burning appliances. A combination unit is a compromise on one of those two placements.

name: Monitoring & Warnings
tagline: A local siren wakes the house. Nothing about it calls anyone.
intro: A standalone smoke alarm makes noise in your hallway. That is its entire external capability. Monitoring adds a path out of the building — to a station that dispatches the fire department whether or not anyone is home to hear it. The argument for it is strongest exactly where it is least glamorous: an empty house, a rental, a second property, a sleeper who cannot self-evacuate. Be aware going in that we could find no study isolating an outcome benefit for residential fire monitoring specifically; the mechanical case is sound, the published evidence is thin, and much of what is written about it is written by people selling it.
buyingNotes: Ask whether the station verifies before dispatching. Residential security-panel monitoring commonly calls you first, which is dead time. A code-compliant fire service in Canada under CAN/ULC-S561 must pass the fire signal to the department within 30 seconds without verification.

Insist on cellular backup. Wi-Fi-only monitoring dies with your router, your power, or the fire itself — which is the moment it was bought for. Several self-monitoring tiers quietly drop cellular entirely.
Check the contract before the hardware. Canadian monitoring is markedly more expensive and more locked-in than American, with three and five-year terms and early termination fees still common.

For an insurance discount in Canada the monitoring generally has to be ULC-certified. A cheap non-ULC contract may earn nothing at all, and no insurer we could find publishes an actual discount figure — you have to ask yours.

Budget for false alarm fees. Many municipalities bill the homeowner for preventable responses, and NIST found that alarms built to the newest standard are still not clearly better at ignoring your cooking.
For wildfire and severe-weather warnings, a weather radio with SAME alerting (NOAA Weather Radio in the US, Weatheradio Canada) keeps working when cell networks are congested.

name: Dry Hydrants & Rural Water Supply
tagline: If there is no hydrant on your road, the water has to come from somewhere.
intro: Past the end of the municipal main, the fire that reaches your house will be fought with whatever water arrives on the truck plus whatever your property can supply. A dry hydrant is the standard answer: a fixed pipe from a pond, stream or buried cistern out to a connection a pumper can draft from at the roadside. It is unglamorous civil engineering, it is usually installed in cooperation with your fire department, and on a rural property it is worth more than almost anything else you could spend the money on — including, in both countries, through the way your area is graded for insurance.
buyingNotes: Physics sets the limit before budget does. A pumper can lift water about 22 ft in ideal conditions, and NFPA 1142 advises designing for no more than 10 to 12 ft of lift. A source below that threshold is worth far more than a bigger one further down a bank.

Volume that counts is pumpable volume, not pond volume. The usable depth runs from the lowest foreseeable water level down to the top of the strainer. NRCS wants at least 30,000 gallons pumpable, or 250 gpm sustained for two hours.

Talk to your fire department before you dig, not after. They have to approve the design, the connection has to match their hard suction thread under NFPA 1963, and they should do the acceptance flow test.

Access is half the installation. All-weather road, room for a loaded pumper to get in and turn, no more than 20 ft of hard suction to the connection, at least 100 ft from any structure, and reflective signage the crew can find at night.

In Canada, the bigger insurance lever is usually your department's Superior Tanker Shuttle Service accreditation rather than your own tank — and an accessible dry hydrant on your land is often part of what gets them there.

name: Residential Fire Sprinklers
tagline: For the fire that starts inside. Not for the one outside.
intro: An NFPA 13D system is a life-safety device: it is designed around one or two heads running for ten minutes, long enough to get everyone out. The evidence behind it is the strongest in home fire safety — NFPA's analysis of five years of US fire data puts the death rate 89% lower and average property loss 55% lower where sprinklers were present. Two things to be clear about before you read further. Only one head operates in 85% of home fires, so the flooding fear is misplaced. And these have essentially nothing to do with wildfire, which attacks the outside of the house; do not let anyone sell you one as wildfire protection.
buyingNotes: Retrofit costs roughly three to four times new construction for the same house, because it means opening finished ceilings. If you are building or doing a gut renovation, this is the only moment the price is reasonable.

The single biggest failure mode is not technical. In NFPA's data, 61% of sprinkler failures were systems that had been shut off before the fire. The most important maintenance task is leaving the control valve open.
A 13D system does not cover your garage, attic or crawlspace — all common fire origins. It is protecting escape routes and living space, not the whole building.

In a cold climate, ask specifically about freezing. Failures concentrate in attics, crawlspaces and exterior wall runs during power outages, and the dry-pipe alternative brings a compressor and more moving parts to maintain.
On a well rather than a municipal main, the stored-water tank and pump needed to meet the ten-minute demand can dominate the budget. Price the water supply before you price the pipework.

name: Kitchen Fire Safety
tagline: Where most home fires start, and where most people do the wrong thing.
intro: Cooking is the leading cause of home fires in both countries, and the most common serious injury comes from moving a burning pan or throwing water into hot oil. Almost everything useful in this category is cheap and low-tech: a lid, a blanket, an extinguisher rated for the right class, and knowing that the correct first move for a pan fire is to smother it and turn off the heat rather than to carry it anywhere.
buyingNotes: A fire blanket beats an extinguisher for a pan fire — no mess, no scatter, and nothing that can blast burning oil across the kitchen. Keep one within reach of the stove but not above it.
Water on burning oil produces a steam explosion that throws flame. This is the single most important thing in this category and it costs nothing to know.

If you buy an extinguisher for the kitchen, understand the class. Standard ABC dry chemical works but coats everything; a wet chemical unit rated for cooking oils is what commercial kitchens use and is far better suited to a deep fryer.
Keep the extinguisher by the exit, not next to the stove. You should never have to reach across a fire to get the thing that puts it out.
A 2.5 lb kitchen extinguisher gives roughly nine seconds of discharge. That is less than it sounds — if it is not out almost immediately, leave.

name: Heating, Woodstoves & Chimneys
tagline: Creosote, clearances, and the inspection nobody books.
intro: Heating equipment is consistently among the leading causes of home fires, and in rural Canada the woodstove is usually the specific thing in question. Almost all of the risk is maintenance and clearance rather than equipment quality: an uninspected flue, a build-up of creosote, combustibles too close to a stove, or ash emptied into a plastic bin on a wooden deck. This is a category where the right purchase is often an appointment rather than a product.
buyingNotes: Book an annual inspection and sweep for any solid-fuel appliance. It is the highest-value thing on this page and it is not something you can safely infer from how the fire looks.
A metal ash can with a tight lid, kept outside and away from the structure, prevents a genuinely common fire. Ash holds live embers for days longer than people expect.
Clearances to combustibles are set by the appliance listing, not by what looks reasonable. If your stove was installed by a previous owner, have the clearances checked.
A chimney fire and a house fire are different events with the same ending. If you have had a chimney fire, the flue needs inspecting before the next fire is lit — the liner may be damaged.

Carbon monoxide belongs in this category as much as fire does. Any fuel-burning appliance means a CO alarm is required in most Canadian jurisdictions, and Ontario extended that to every storey as of January 2026.

name: Electrical Fire Safety
tagline: Arc faults, old panels, and the extension cord under the rug.
intro: Electrical distribution and lighting equipment causes a large share of home fires and a disproportionate share of the deadly ones, because they start inside walls and in spaces nobody is watching. The products that help are mostly code-driven rather than consumer-driven — arc-fault protection, proper panel work, surge protection — and the useful consumer behaviour is mostly about load, damage and age rather than gadgets.
buyingNotes: Arc-fault circuit interrupters detect the kind of arcing that a standard breaker ignores, and are required for most living-space circuits in new construction in both countries. Retrofitting them into an older panel is a real and worthwhile upgrade.
Extension cords are temporary by design. Running one under a rug or through a doorway damages the insulation and traps heat, and permanent use of one is a sign you need an outlet, not a longer cord.
Old and recalled panels are worth identifying. If your house still has a panel type with a known failure history, an electrician's assessment is money well spent.
Space heaters cause more fires than almost any other appliance, and the rule is the simple one: nothing combustible within a metre, plugged directly into a wall outlet, never into a power bar.

Lithium battery fires — e-bikes, scooters, tool packs — are a fast-growing category. Charge them away from exits and sleeping areas, and stop using any pack that is swollen, damaged or has been in a crash.

name: Escape Planning & Egress
tagline: Two ways out of every room, practised once, in the dark.
intro: Modern furnishings burn faster than the ones the old escape-time research was based on, which is why the advice has moved from 'get out' to 'get out quickly, and know how before it happens'. The equipment here is minimal — an escape ladder for a second storey, a torch where you can find it — and the thing that matters most is free: a plan everyone in the house has actually walked through, including whoever cannot get themselves out.
buyingNotes: Escape ladders are the one real purchase. Buy one per upstairs bedroom, not one for the house, and check it reaches the ground from that window.
Practise it once with the ladder actually deployed. Almost nobody does, and an unpractised ladder at 2 a.m. in smoke is close to useless.
Agree a meeting point outside and make it specific — a particular tree or the neighbour's driveway, not 'out front'. The counting happens there, and nobody goes back in.
Plan for whoever needs help: small children, anyone with mobility limits, and pets. Assign a person, and have a backup for when that person is away.
Sleep with bedroom doors closed. A closed door meaningfully slows fire and smoke spread, and it is the single most effective free thing in this category.

name: Commercial Sprinkler Systems
tagline: The system that does most of the work in a commercial fire, and the one that costs most to get wrong.
intro: Automatic sprinklers control or put out most fires in buildings that have them, and in most new commercial, institutional and multi-unit residential construction they are required by the building code rather than chosen. What you are actually choosing is the type: wet-pipe for heated space, dry-pipe or pre-action where pipes would freeze or water damage is the bigger fear, ESFR for high-piled storage, deluge for fast-spreading industrial hazards. A licensed sprinkler contractor designs the system to NFPA 13 (or 13R for low-rise residential), and the building code that adopts it differs by province and state. None of this is bought off a shelf.
buyingNotes: Start with the occupancy and the water supply, not the hardware. A hydraulic calculation against a current flow test decides whether you need a fire pump, and the pump is often the biggest line item in a retrofit.

Get the design basis in writing: which edition of NFPA 13 or 13R, which hazard classification, and what commodity and storage height it assumes. Changing what you store later can quietly invalidate it.
Inspection, testing and maintenance follow NFPA 25 in both countries. Budget for it from day one: quarterly, annual and five-year tasks, plus antifreeze and dry-pipe work where they apply.
The most common sprinkler failure is a closed valve. Supervise or lock control valves and treat a closed valve as an emergency, not a maintenance note.

Get at least two quotes from licensed contractors, and check the licence yourself: ASTTBC registration in BC, the RBQ licence in Quebec, NICET-certified designers and a state fire protection licence such as California's C-16 in the US.

name: Commercial Kitchen Fire Suppression
tagline: Required over grease-producing cooking, and only as good as its last six-month service.
intro: Restaurant and institutional kitchens are one of the few places where the codes are completely clear: a hood over grease-producing appliances needs a listed fire suppression system, the system has to meet UL 300 in the US (ULC/ORD-C1254.6 in Canada), and it has to be inspected every six months. The system is a pre-engineered wet-chemical unit that sprays a potassium-salt agent onto the appliances and into the duct, shuts off the fuel, and is backed up by a Class K portable extinguisher on the wall. You buy it from an authorized distributor of the brand, who designs, installs and services it.
buyingNotes: Systems older than the UL 300 standard (1994) were designed for animal fats, not today's high-temperature vegetable oils. If a kitchen still has one, replacing it is not optional in most jurisdictions.
Rearranging or swapping appliances under the hood can leave them outside nozzle coverage. Tell your service company before the line changes, not after.
Semi-annual inspection is required, and fusible links have to be replaced on a fixed schedule. Keep the tags; inspectors and insurers ask for them.
The Class K extinguisher is a backup for after the system has fired, not a substitute for it.
Hood and duct cleaning is a separate trade and a separate schedule. Grease in the duct is what turns a pan fire into a building fire.

name: Special Hazard & Clean Agent Systems
tagline: For rooms where water would do more damage than the fire: server rooms, archives, switchgear, flammable liquids.
intro: Special hazard systems put out fires with something other than ordinary sprinkler water: a clean agent gas, inert gas, water mist, condensed aerosol, foam, CO2 or dry chemical. Each suits a different risk, and several are in the middle of a regulatory transition. 3M stopped making Novec 1230 at the end of 2025, US rules now push HFC-227ea (FM-200) toward recycled supply, and PFAS-based firefighting foams are being restricted in Canada and most US states. These systems are engineered and installed by authorized distributors, and the decision usually involves your insurer, a fire protection engineer and the authority having jurisdiction.
buyingNotes: Decide what you are protecting first: business continuity of electronics, people in the room, or a flammable-liquid process. The answer usually picks the agent.
Total-flooding gas systems only work if the room holds the agent. Room integrity (a door-fan test) and sealing penetrations are part of the job, and remodels break it.
Ask who supplies the agent for recharges over the life of the system, and get it in writing. Agent supply is changing faster than hardware lifespans.
CO2 total flooding can kill people in the protected space. It belongs in normally unoccupied spaces with lockouts, warning signs and training.
Many of these hazards still need sprinklers as well. A clean agent system protects the equipment; the building code may still require sprinklers for the building.

name: Equipment & Vehicle Suppression
tagline: Small automatic systems that live inside the cabinet, machine or engine bay where the fire starts.
intro: Some fires start inside an enclosure: an electrical cabinet, a CNC machine, a fume hood, the engine compartment of a bus or loader. Room-level systems either cannot reach them or would flood a whole building to deal with a box. Local-application systems put detection and agent right at the source, usually with a pressurised tube that bursts at the hot spot and needs no electrical power. They are bought through the makers' distributors and are often driven by insurers or fleet operators rather than building codes.
buyingNotes: Match the agent to the equipment: clean agent for electronics, dry chemical or foam where fuel and hydraulic fluid are involved.
Ask for the listing or approval that applies to your use. Approvals differ between cabinet systems and vehicle systems, and not every product carries one.
These systems still need periodic inspection. Detection tubing ages, and a system that has quietly lost pressure protects nothing.
For vehicles and mobile equipment, check what your insurer, fleet contract or transit authority requires before choosing a brand.

name: Commercial Fire Alarm & Detection
tagline: The panel, the devices on the ceiling, and the line out to the monitoring station.
intro: A commercial fire alarm system is not a bigger home smoke alarm. It is a control panel, a network of detectors, pull stations and horn-strobes, and a connection to a monitoring station, all designed and verified to NFPA 72 in the US and to the CAN/ULC-S524 installation and S537 verification standards in Canada, then inspected every year (CAN/ULC-S536 in Canada; Ontario moved to the 2019 edition on 1 January 2026). The panel you choose sets your service costs for years, and specialist detection such as air-sampling, beam and flame detectors exists for spaces ordinary spot detectors handle badly.
buyingNotes: Addressable panels cost more up front but identify the exact device in alarm or trouble. For anything beyond a very small building they are usually worth it.
Ask whether the panel is proprietary, meaning only one dealer can service it. Proprietary panels lock you to one service company for the life of the system.
Copper phone lines are being retired. If your panel still reports over POTS lines, budget for a cellular or IP communicator now, not after a failed test.
Annual inspection and testing is required in both countries. Keep the reports: insurers and fire inspectors ask for them.
In Canada, fire alarm monitoring that counts for code purposes has to go to a station listed to CAN/ULC-S561. In the US, look for a UL-listed central station.

name: Portable Extinguishers for Business
tagline: Required in almost every workplace, and specific to what can burn there.
intro: Portable extinguishers are the one piece of business fire protection you can buy over the counter, but what you need, how many, and where they hang is set by the fire code: NFPA 10 in the US, and NFPA 10 adopted through the National Fire Code of Canada and provincial codes. The right extinguisher depends on the fire class: ABC dry chemical for general use, CO2 or clean agent where residue would ruin equipment, Class K in kitchens, Class D for combustible metals. Most businesses buy and service them through a local fire equipment company, which also does the required monthly-check tags and annual maintenance.
buyingNotes: Size and spacing come from NFPA 10, by hazard and floor area. A fire equipment company will lay them out; a big-box store will not.
Annual maintenance by a qualified technician is required, plus periodic internal examination and hydrostatic testing that depends on the extinguisher type.
Do not use water or foam on energised electrical equipment unless the unit is rated for it. Water mist extinguishers carry a C rating; ordinary water does not.
Be sceptical of 'lithium-ion' extinguishers. There is no recognised North American performance standard for them yet.
Training matters as much as the hardware. Workplace safety rules in both countries expect staff who are expected to use extinguishers to be trained.

name: Emergency Lighting, Exit Signs & Fire Doors
tagline: The unglamorous parts of a building that decide whether people find the way out.
intro: Emergency lights, exit signs and fire doors are passive, cheap per unit and routinely neglected. Exit signs differ between the two countries: Canada's building code has required the green running-man pictogram in new construction since 2010, while most US jurisdictions still use red or green EXIT wording. Fire doors and the closers, latches and hold-open devices on them are part of a rated assembly, and a wedge under one breaks it. These are bought through electrical wholesalers, door-hardware suppliers and fire equipment companies, and inspected on a fixed schedule.
buyingNotes: Test emergency lighting monthly and do a full-duration test annually. Batteries are the usual failure.
Buy the sign your jurisdiction requires. A red EXIT sign is non-compliant in new Canadian construction.
Never wedge a fire door open. If it needs to stay open, fit a listed hold-open device that releases on alarm.
Fire door assemblies are inspected annually under NFPA 80. Damaged closers, missing latches and added hardware are the usual failures.

name: Battery & EV Fire Safety
tagline: A fast-growing hazard where the products are ahead of the standards.
intro: Lithium-ion batteries in tools, scooters, e-bikes, energy storage and vehicles fail differently from ordinary fires: thermal runaway generates its own heat and flammable gases and can reignite hours later. Storage cabinets, charging rules and EV fire blankets are sensible tools, but much of the market is ahead of the standards, and some claims are not backed by any recognised test. Treat this category as risk reduction around storage, charging and separation, not as a product that makes the risk go away.
buyingNotes: Charge and store packs away from exits and combustibles, and stop using any battery that is swollen, damaged or has been in a crash.
Ask storage-cabinet makers what test the cabinet was built to and for a copy of the report. A metal box is not automatically a fire-rated one.
EV fire blankets are a containment tool for trained responders, not an extinguisher.
Large battery energy storage installations fall under NFPA 855 in the US and electrical and fire code rules in Canada. Involve the authority having jurisdiction early.
